faq: What does this tool calculate?
Degrees multiplied by π/180 — radians, at full precision, sign preserved.
Is the calculation done locally?
Yes — instantly in your browser.
How accurate is the result?
Exact factor, float precision — the conversion contributes no error worth discussing; wrong-unit inputs are the real hazard.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
Angles are datum-free; the coordinates this site serves are WGS84.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
Radians for code should keep full precision — rounding angles early compounds through trig. Display rounding is for humans, not pipelines.
Reverse conversion?
Multiply by 180/π — the Coordinate Converter family and a radians-to-degrees lane handle the return trip.
Why do libraries use radians?
Because calculus makes radians natural: the derivative of sine is cosine only in radians. Two centuries of mathematics voted; code complies.
Bearings over 360°?
They convert fine (450° = 7.854 rad) — normalising to a revolution is your code's choice, not the conversion's.
Gradians?
The 400-per-circle survey unit exists; this converter's lane is the degree-radian pair the world runs on.
Small angles?
For tiny angles, radians ≈ the angle's sine and tangent — the approximation astronomers live by, visible in the converter's output.
DMS input?
Convert DMS to decimal degrees first (DMS to Decimal), then to radians — two clean steps beat one muddy one.
